newsitem.title: USA: Senator sees White House wavering on smog standards.
newsitem.headline: Senator sees White House wavering on smog standards.

text.p: The White House is becoming more concerned that an Environmental Protection Agency proposal to tighten air quality standards could present big economic and political problems, a Democratic senator said Friday.
"I think the recognition of this as a political problem has been elevated," Louisiana Sen. John Breaux said.
"I think we're making some real progress in getting them to see the error of what they're trying to do," he told reporters after addressing an oil industry group.

Breaux said he has had meetings with White House officials on the issue, and sees dissent within the administration on the EPA proposal, which has drawn a storm of protest from industries as well as from many states and communties.
The EPA proposed tightening the standards for smog and soot in November, sparking a massive lobbying contest between environmental and health advocates and industry groups.
EPA Administrator Carol Browner is to make her final recommendation to the White House on the standards later this month, and the administration is to announce a final rule in July.

Breaux, whose oil-producing state would be hit by stricter air pollution standards, said he hoped the administration would "work something out" to change or drop the proposal. If not, he said, Congress could move legislation to extend the deadline for setting the rule.
Browner, who has met with the Senate Democratic Caucus, is "starting to understand this does not have a great deal of support in Congress," Breaux said.
But at a House hearing Thursday, Browner said there is a great deal of public support for stricter standards and said her proposal was based on "our reading of the best available science."
She added, however, that she had not made a final decision.

Letters have been circulating among both parties in the House and Senate urging the administration to hold off on imposing stricter air standards, which a number of legislators said would be unreasonably costly to meet and could cause a backlash against environmental laws.

Earlier Friday, Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott told the same industry group, the Independent Petroleum Association of America, that he, Breaux and others will make a "bipartisan effort to keep this EPA assault from going into effect."
Lott, of Mississippi, said the proposal would be "a real detriment to business and industry all over the country."
